extracted.intended_audience: educators, school administrators, and policymakers interested in industrial/technical/vocational education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for organizing technical/industrial schools and apprenticeships (workshop-in-school, school-in-workshop models), including curriculum balance, admissions, duration, pedagogic methods, incentives, facilities, and outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal certification for practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice of surgeons (and female surgeons) was forbidden for those who failed to pass a satisfactory examination before the proper authorities (document dated 1311).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal examination and formal certification were treated as necessary for legitimate practice; historical edicts (e.g., 1311, King John 1352) show practice under legal authority is a criterion of legitimate professional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic recognition via degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities (Cordova, Salamanca, Alcala, etc.) honored many women with doctors' degrees; such academic degrees recognized and legitimated the practitioner's status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting of university doctorates is presented as a mark of qualification and social/legal acceptance; published learned works (even if pseudonymous) were associated with scholarly legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill, learning, and reputation as measures of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals became 'eminent for her skill and learning' (example: Frau Erxleben) and commanded respect and a large practice; reputation and documented success were indicators of professional standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical evidence (practice success, pupils' subsequent careers) is used as a metric of a practitioner's effectiveness and contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational model: workshop-in-school vs school-in-workshop
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasting types are described: atelier dans l'école (workshop in the school) and the school in the workshop; each model shapes how mental/scientific training and manual labor are combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select model according to objectives: 'workshop in school' favors broader schooling with supervised shop work; 'school in workshop' immerses apprentices in commercial/industrial environment with formal instruction adjunct to production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating diverse technical schools as a single 'Continental system'
rubrics_metrics.description: The article warns against mentally throwing together the diverse Continental technical and polytechnic schools as one system — their organization and aims differ widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of methods should account for type-specific aims and results (Polytechnicum vs horological school vs pedagogic school), not assume uniform practices or outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation system in early training
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecole Communale uses rotation: pupils spend one day in carpentry, another forging, another metal-turning, etc.; extreme division of labor is viewed as prejudicial at this stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotation cultivates general intelligence and broad skills, delaying specialization to develop faculties rather than quick manual dexterity; recommended for very young pupils (as young as 8–9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hours: proportion of lessons to manual labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Ecole Communale gives only an hour and a half each morning and afternoon to manual labor (most of day to lessons); Institution de Saint Nicolas devotes most of the day to manual work with limited schooling hours; Ecole Municipale gives five hours studies and six hours shop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time allocation should reflect institutional aims: foundational intelligence vs rapid production-readiness. Explicit schedules are part of evaluating school design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work always done from prior drawings and models
rubrics_metrics.description: Every pupil works from drawings previously made to scale; exercises are directed by sketches — whether making joints, turning cylinders, or filing nuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize drafting and model-making as integral to shop practice: 'it is always done according to a careful sketch made beforehand' to develop planning, measurement, and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid commercial production in elementary training
rubrics_metrics.description: At Ecole Communale 'no articles whatever are made for sale' and 'all commercial elements are scrupulously avoided' to focus on training rather than market pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-commercial exercises (e.g., geometric models, small accurate joints) prioritize learning over meeting commercial deadlines or profitability, allowing slower pace and pedagogic variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce marketable work in advanced/apprenticed settings
rubrics_metrics.description: At Institution de Saint Nicolas and Chaix et Cie, pupils produce salable goods; masters provide materials and the objects made are of the same character as ordinary apprentices' work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercially oriented workshops teach value of materials, time, and produce readiness for trade — suitable where aim is immediate employability and understanding of market exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission prerequisites (literacy and basic schooling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Saint Nicolas admits none who cannot already read and write; Ecole Municipale admits only after primary education is completed and often after an easy examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set minimum literacy and elementary education requirements to ensure pupils can benefit from technical/theoretical instruction (drawing, geometry, written lessons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master-led ateliers with real masters/foremen
rubrics_metrics.description: Each atelier is let to an approved master or patron who supervises apprentices, provides materials, and often owns separate businesses; foremen take pride in instruction and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instruction by skilled masters links training to authentic trade practices; having masters/foremen invested in pupil success improves quality and placement outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation / boarding as a pedagogic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Institution de Saint Nicolas values 'complete isolation from exterior influences' via internment (boarders) to focus pupils on training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boarding and controlled environments can concentrate learning and ensure discipline, but entail parental financial contributions and institutional costs; weigh benefits vs inclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive curriculum integrating general and technical subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Courses include drawing, model-making, grammar, composition, reading proofs, types, engraving, history of printing, economics, mechanics, physics, chemistry, and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend liberal and technical education so apprentices gain intellectual tools (language, economics, science) alongside trade skills — supports long-term adaptability and leadership potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured progression and apprenticeship duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical apprenticeship terms mentioned are three to four years; first years often exploratory (rotation/rounding), later years settle into a single pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define multi-year curricula with an initial broad foundation year followed by specialization; three- to four-year terms are presented as effective durations to produce competent workmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time/earnings incentives and financial arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Apprentices may earn rising wages (e.g., 50 centimes to 2.5 francs), gratuities, or participate in profit-sharing (Chaix et Cie), and are encouraged to save via a savings bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wages, gratifications, profit participation, and savings schemes foster loyalty, prudence, and an appreciation of 'time is money'; financial incentives can reduce labor unrest and encourage retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic technical drawing and measurement training
rubrics_metrics.description: Apprentices learn to sketch machinery from actual measurement, then draw carefully to scale with rule and compass; solid geometry is 'excellently conceived and admirably followed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous training in measurement, geometry, and technical drawing is essential for producing 'intelligent workmen' capable of designing, interpreting, and executing precise work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early general training before specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Pupils spend initial years sampling various shops (a fortnight in each) so there is 'no haste to specialize' and they may discover the pursuit for which they are best fitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delayed specialization allows informed trade choice and broader skill sets, beneficial for adolescents still developing aptitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on producing 'intelligent workmen' rather than mere dexterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors prefer 'cultivating their intelligence to quickening mere manual dexterity'; the goal is to make educated, steady, and skilled workmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize conceptual understanding, planning, and technical knowledge alongside manual skills to enable career progression (foreman/master) and adaptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilities and supporting infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective schools feature galleries/museums of pupils' work, spacious refectories, well-ventilated dormitories, gymnasium, drawing/modeling galleries, and well-equipped workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical resources and exhibition of student work contribute to morale, standards, and public recognition — they are part of institutional quality and should be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment via measurable outcomes (employment, wages, advancement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success is reported as employment rates after course completion, average wages earned (e.g., 4 francs/day), and career progression to foreman or master; high placement and earnings used as evidence of efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use post-training employment statistics, earnings, and long-term career outcomes as objective metrics to evaluate program effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with industry and direct pathways to employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Chaix et Cie. recruits most apprentices into firm employment and profit-sharing; many former pupils become depositors or insured employees; masters often place pupils in employers' shops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close ties with industry (in-house apprenticeships, commission work, employer networks) strengthen transition to employment and can be considered a criterion of program success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal/inspector involvement and systematic management
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspectors and directors (e.g., M. Berger, M. Laubier, M. Muller) actively design curricula, conduct scientific instruction, and organize systems (rotation, drawing, shop supervision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong, informed leadership and systematic oversight (curriculum design, inspectorate) are necessary for consistent quality and institutional improvement.
